simple: Software that is known to boot on this exact board, run first as a reference before any of your own code.
analogy: One day in the new building exactly as the last principal left it, working, to watch and copy before moving in.
precise: A boot stack (vendor or mainline loader and OS, or firmware alone) whose serial log, devicetree and kernel log are captured as the baseline that every later difference is measured against (curriculum 11.5, step 3). In BR-07's lab: OpenSBI as shipped with QEMU on the sifive_u board model.
source: C1 of BR-07 (Systems Curriculum 11.5; a map, pending verification); R1 of BR-07 (lab run)

simple: A list, made from a board's devicetree, of what every device needs before it can work.
analogy: The list of light switches, keys and door signs for every room, written before moving in.
precise: This course's name for the output of BR-07's bringup_deps tool: for each devicetree node with a compatible string, its status, its first reg entry translated to a CPU address through every ranges above it, and its providers (clocks, resets, pin groups, supplies, power domains, interrupt parent, GPIOs, DMA channels, dma-coherent), followed by a stage order in which every provider precedes its consumers. It is an input to the bring-up plan, not the plan.
source: BR-07 Listing 1 and runs R6–R9 (this build); property meanings after D1 and D2 of BR-07 (pending verification)

simple: Pins or fuses that tell a chip's boot ROM where to look for the next program.
analogy: A note on the school gate saying where today's keys are kept.
precise: Inputs sampled at reset (on some SoCs, fuses) whose value selects the boot medium and mode the boot ROM uses, for example SD card, eMMC, SPI flash or a USB recovery mode; the SiFive FU540 calls them MSEL. A second selectable source is what makes a recovery path possible.
source: D4 of BR-07 (SiFive FU540-C000 Manual, title only, pending verification); C1 of BR-07 (curriculum 11.1, 11.2); R2 of BR-07 (QEMU's own option text)

simple: The part that provides one voltage to one group of devices, which software may have to switch on.
analogy: A room's own heating circuit, which must be on before anyone can work there.
precise: A voltage regulator described as a devicetree node; a consumer names it with a property whose name ends in -supply (for example vmmc-supply), and the OS's regulator driver enables it and sets its voltage before the consumer is used. With the supply off, no register write inside the consumer can work.
source: D2 of BR-07 (Linux kernel documentation, regulator bindings; title only, pending verification)

simple: A part of a chip whose power can be switched on and off as a whole.
analogy: A wing of the building on its own fuse.
precise: A region of an SoC behind a power switch; a power-controller node with #power-domain-cells provides it and a consumer names it with power-domains. While the domain is off, the blocks inside it do not respond; the OS powers it before probing them and may power it down when idle.
source: D2 of BR-07 (Linux kernel documentation, power-domain bindings; title only, pending verification)

simple: A word in a device's devicetree entry saying that the device sees what the CPU caches hold when it reads or writes memory.
analogy: A delivery truck that checks the teacher's desk as well as the storeroom before loading boxes.
precise: A devicetree property marking a device whose DMA accesses are coherent with the CPU caches, so the OS needs no cache clean or invalidate around its transfers. What a missing property implies is an architecture and OS convention (RISC-V also defines dma-noncoherent; recalled, unverified), so its absence is a question for the SoC manual, not an answer.
source: D1 and D2 of BR-07 (Devicetree Specification; Linux DMA documentation; title only, pending verification); R6, R8 and R16 of BR-07 (lab runs)
